name: Looksmax.org / forum participation

lead: Looksmax.org is described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing, alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com. Members post photos for feedback, ask for ratings and share guides, using the replies as a map for what to improve in their face and body.

The chain is simple: post photos, get a current and 'potential' PSL score from peers, read the shared guides, then apply tips on skin, grooming, fitness or procedures. The feedback comes from peers on a self-devised rating scale, and the guides' methods range from studied to anecdotal.

paras: Members typically post front and side photos, discuss softmaxxing (non-invasive changes) and hardmaxxing (surgery, steroids), and use shared vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes. Many post progress photos over months to track changes. Anonymity is common.

Commentators and researchers link the subculture to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety, promotion of dangerous methods, blackpill determinism and radicalisation. Critics also call the PSL scale unscientific and biased against non-white men. Members often gatekeep against casual 'normies'.

web.title: Inside the Disturbing Forum Incels Use to Brutally Criticize Each Other's Faces
Looksmaxxing is the disturbing TikTok trend

chain: Post photos and get PSL ratings
Apply tips to face and body
angle.text: Members post progress photos, request ratings and swap guides, using the feedback and shared methods as a map for improving face and body. The ratings come from peers on a self-devised scale, and the guides' methods vary from studied to anecdotal.

lead: Looksmax.org is an online forum devoted to improving male appearance, described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com.[1] Members use it to get outside feedback on how they look and to find guides on what to change: they post photos in rating threads, track progress photos over months, and read or write guides covering skincare, grooming, hair, fitness, posture and, for some, surgery and medical treatments.[2][1]

Participation follows a loop that members describe in their own terms: post photos and questions, receive ratings and critiques (often a current and a 'potential' PSL score), apply changes such as skincare, a haircut, fitness or procedures, and post follow-up photos.[1][3] The forum belongs to a lineage of appearance-focused boards, including Lookism.net, whose rate-me threads were profiled by Vice in 2018.[4]

The forum has published its own member surveys. Its 2025 survey, covering respondents with fewer than 1,000 posts (1,593 responses), reported about 62 percent under 18, roughly 90 percent under 21, and about 99.5 percent male.[5] Researchers who have studied comparable looksmaxxing boards describe both the self-improvement content and the harsh rating culture, and these findings are covered below.[3]
infobox: Guides, PSL rating threads, progress photos
Independent forums after 2017, TikTok from about 2020

paras: The forum is organised as a conventional message board with sections for guides, rating requests, progress logs and general discussion. Members write under anonymous handles. Typical threads ask for an assessment of a face or physique, compare techniques, or report results of a skincare routine, a diet, a haircut or a procedure.[1][4]

Content spans what the community calls softmaxxing (non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness, plus practices such as mewing) and hardmaxxing (surgery, drugs and other invasive measures).[2] Female-oriented guides reportedly began appearing on the forum in 2024 and 2025.[1]

Wikipedia reports that looksmaxxing was coined and developed on incel and manosphere message boards in the 2010s, naming PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net as the 'PSL forums' that devised the PSL rating scale of facial attractiveness.[2] A 2018 Vice report on Lookism.net, by Allie Conti, described a board where members posted selfies in 'rate-me' threads and received suggestions ranging from hairstyles to jaw and chin implants, rhinoplasty and forehead reduction. It reported one long-time member with nearly 13,000 posts since 2015 and about 600 users active at once on a typical day.[4]

After Reddit banned r/incels in 2017, activity moved to independent forums, often on.is domains, and from around 2020 to TikTok, where it reached audiences outside incel circles.[1] Wikipedia describes early TikTok videos as often framing looksmaxxing as self-improvement with self-deprecating humor, with black pill ideology becoming more associated with it in mainstream discourse by the mid-2020s.[2] Looksmax.org has marked anniversaries with community events, including a sixth-anniversary raffle in 2024.[6]

Members post progress photos and request ratings on current and potential PSL, sometimes using wet-hair photos to reduce styling effects.[1] Ratings are competitive and quantify perceived genetic potential.[1] Anonymity is common, and members gatekeep against casual 'normies'.[1] Core vocabulary includes softmaxxing, hardmaxxing, blackpill, canthal tilt, hunter eyes, mewing and bonesmashing.[2][1]

Members compare the forum with its Discord server. In one forum thread, one reply recommended the Discord as a friendlier service, while another described it as full of users who are there for rating.[7] Vice's 2018 profile of a related board found members describing it as either addictive or as a judgment-free place to post controversial opinions.[4]

The 2025 survey summary, posted by the forum's administrators, reported that most respondents were very young and almost entirely male, with about 42 percent between 170 and 179 cm tall and about 39 percent between 180 and 189 cm, and North America the largest region. It separated users with fewer than 1,000 posts (80 percent or more of responses) from heavier posters.[5] Earlier annual survey threads exist for 2024.[8]

Halpin and colleagues (2025, Sociology of Health & Illness) qualitatively analysed 8,072 comments from two looksmaxxing boards sampled in 2023: a forum on fitness, style and surgery (5,327 comments) and a ratings forum (2,745 comments). The authors reported a 'hegemonic masculine gaze' in which ratings tended to demean rather than advise, interventions such as mewing, bonesmashing, leg-lengthening and cosmetic procedures pursued to close perceived gaps, and praise concentrated on men who matched the community's ideals. They also reported dozens of instances of users encouraging self-harm or suicide.[3] The paper does not name the sites, and it notes limitations including self-reported posts and a sample favouring active threads.[3]

In The Conversation (January 2024), psychologist Jamilla Rosdahl wrote that looksmaxxing content on TikTok targets insecure young men, can progress from grooming to extreme measures, and may route viewers toward incel communities through platform recommendations; she framed it as a response to wider pressures such as economic insecurity and anxiety.[9] Vice's 2018 report quoted experts who said such boards could intensify body-dysmorphic concerns in vulnerable users.[4] Wikipedia also records that some men report benefits such as dating success and peer praise.[2]

Commentators describe the practice as judgemental and link it to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and researchers say it promotes hegemonic masculinity.[2] Wikipedia also reports that doctors have criticized mewing and bonesmashing as misinformation.[2]

Grokipedia lists controversies including blackpill determinism, misogynistic slang, promotion of unproven methods such as bonesmashing and unregulated overseas surgery with reported complications, criticism of PSL as unscientific, and research linking the subculture to radicalisation.[1]

No studies found. Published research on this forum itself is limited to qualitative analyses of looksmaxxing boards generally, described above.[3] Studies of other online communities, such as analyses of weight-loss subreddits, concern different groups.[10]

lore.intro: Within the forum and in commentary about it, participation is described both as a route to self-improvement and as a competitive rating culture.[1][7][3]
